purpose: Belatacept is used to help prevent your body from rejecting a transplanted kidney. It works alongside other medicines to keep your immune system from attacking your new kidney. It is only used in adults who have received a kidney transplant.
how_it_works: Your immune system has special cells called T-cells that can mistakenly attack a transplanted organ as if it were a foreign invader. Belatacept blocks a signal that activates those T-cells, so they are less likely to attack your new kidney. Think of it like cutting the 'on switch' for the immune cells that cause rejection.
common_side_effects: Common side effects include anemia (low red blood cells), swelling in your hands or feet, high blood pressure, nausea, diarrhea, headache, urinary tract infections, and feeling tired. Some people may also notice changes in kidney function lab values.
warnings: Important: Belatacept can increase your risk of serious infections because it lowers your immune defenses. It also carries a rare but serious risk of a brain infection called PML and certain cancers, especially a lymphoma linked to the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). For this reason, it should only be used in patients who have been exposed to EBV before. You should avoid live vaccines while taking this medicine. Always tell your doctor right away if you notice any unusual symptoms, confusion, or new lumps.
typical_dosing: Belatacept is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) at your doctor's office or clinic — you cannot take it at home as a pill. The dose is based on your body weight. It is given more frequently at first (every two weeks for the first few months), and then once a month for as long as you need it. Each infusion takes about 30 minutes.
